notes:
I found verse-by-verse sources for all 22 verses. Each section has the usual reading first, then any real differences between interpreters. A few gaps, listed at the end, came from running out of searches.

**The chapter as a whole.** Keil (as quoted by Constable) says this poem differs from chapters 1–2 mainly because it presents the disaster as a well-merited punishment by God for the grievous sins of the inhabitants of Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html

---

**v. 1**
- *The usual reading:* Guzik says gold doesn't tarnish, but it loses its shine under dust. He quotes Ryken that this is what happened to the temple's gold objects, trampled in the city's dusty streets. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
- Constable reads it both ways. The temple's gold and gems no longer adorned it, and Jeremiah also compares Jerusalem's people to gold and gems now lying dead in the streets. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html
- *Interpreters differ: literal temple treasure or people?*
  - Poole: the most and best interpreters take it in its native sense, for the gold which adorned the temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/4-1.htm
  - The Geneva notes read it as a picture: By the gold he means the princes, as by the stones he understands the priests. (same URL)
  - Gill (Baptist) allows a hint of the temple gold but says it should be read figuratively, of God's people. He adds a pastoral point: gold can lose its shine but not its nature, as believers can decline without being lost. (same URL)
  - Keil and Delitzsch say the verse must be figurative. The chapter mourns the fate of people, not buildings. (same URL)
  - The Pulpit Commentary says holy jewels would never really have been thrown into the street, so that line is a figure of speech. (same URL)
- *Modern scholarly notes:* The Cambridge Bible says the Hebrew verb is irregular. With small changes some scholars read "become hateful" or "How is the ancient gold become dim." (same URL)

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the generation taken to Babylon was valued there no more than clay pots. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
- Constable: clay pottery was worth so little that people simply replaced it instead of mending it, and the Babylonians had smashed many of Jerusalem's people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html
- Clarke (Methodist): they were once of the *pure standard* of holiness but are now dishonoured vessels. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-4.html
- JFB: because these "sons of Zion" defiled their gold with worldliness, God justly treated them as clay pots. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/lamentations-4.html

**v. 3**
- Guzik: the people seemed worse than jackals, more like ostriches, which were thought to be cruel to their young. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
- Constable: the siege turned once-caring women selfish. Like ostriches (Job 39:14–18), they abandoned and even ate their children. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html
- Clarke on the KJV's "sea monsters": the Hebrew *tannin* means any large, fierce creature, on land or in the sea. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-4.html
- Calvin reads the word as the young of serpents, treated more kindly than the Jews. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/lamentations-4.html

**v. 4**
- Calvin: mothers would gladly give their own blood to feed their babies, so a child's tongue sticking to its mouth from thirst seemed almost beyond nature. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/lamentations-4.html
- Constable: the infants went without because parents looked after their own needs first. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html
- Guzik quotes Harrison that the author must have seen these scenes himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/

**v. 5**
- Guzik: no one escaped, and those once high were brought very low. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
- Clarke: they lay on straw or rubbish instead of costly carpets and sofas. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-4.html
- Constable: the wealthy went to the ash heaps probably because they were sick (compare Job 2:8). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html

**v. 6**
- *The usual reading:* Sodom fell in a moment; Jerusalem suffered slowly.
  - Clarke: Jerusalem fell by the most *lingering* calamities. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-4.html
  - Guzik links this to Ezekiel 16:48–49: Jerusalem's sin was worse than Sodom's, so its punishment was greater too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
- *More privilege, more guilt:*
  - Matthew Henry: Sodom never had God's word and prophets as Jerusalem did, so Jerusalem's condemnation is more severe (Matthew 11:23–24). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_004.cfm
  - JFB: no prophets were sent to Sodom as they were to Judea. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/lamentations-4.html
- *Is the poet complaining?*
  - Calvin (Reformed): the prophet was not arguing with God or calling Him too harsh. He was calling the Jews to see that they deserved it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/lamentations-4.html
  - Coffman (Churches of Christ): Israel's ordeal lasted seventy years, starting with the siege. He says God spared Israel only because of the promise of the Messiah through Abraham. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/lamentations-4.html

**v. 7**
- *Who are "her dignitaries" (KJV "Nazarites")?*
  - Guzik: Most all commentators agree this does not mean people under the Nazirite vow but leaders and notable people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
  - Constable instead says some of these people had dedicated themselves to the Lord and were of the highest quality. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html
  - Matthew Henry speaks of those "separated to God" being caught up in the common disaster. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_004.cfm
- Clarke: the "sapphire" may describe blue veins under the skin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-4.html

**v. 8**
- Guzik quotes Harrison that the nobles can't be recognised because famine reduced everyone to a common level of physical exhaustion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
- Matthew Henry: their skin became as dry and hard as wood. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_004.cfm

**v. 9**
- Constable: those killed by the sword were more fortunate, because a quick death is better than a slow one. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html
- JFB: "pine away" is literally "flow out." Sword language is borrowed to show that famine is the sword by which their blood flows. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/lamentations-4.html
- Matthew Henry, pastorally: those who are ready for the next world need not fear a short passage there. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_004.cfm

**v. 10**
- Constable: once-caring women boiled and ate their children to survive the siege (compare Lamentations 2:20; 2 Kings 6:25–29; Jeremiah 19:9). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html
- Guzik: this is why Zion's agony was worse than Sodom's. He quotes Trapp, who says they boiled rather than roasted so the smell wouldn't give them away, as later happened in the Roman siege. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/

**v. 11**
- Guzik: Jeremiah saw God's fierce anger "fulfilled" on Zion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
- Calvin: God is content with moderate punishment if people wake up, but when He pours out His wrath, there is no hope of repentance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/lamentations-4.html
- Constable: ironically, God consumed the city with literal fire. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html

**v. 12**
- Constable: Jerusalem had been invaded before but had strengthened its defences and seemed impregnable. He quotes Chisholm that sinful people, even if outwardly associated with the covenant community, should not take God's protection for granted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html
- Calvin: since no nation thought it possible, the city fell by God's hand rather than by enemy strength. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/lamentations-4.html

**v. 13**
- *The usual reading:*
  - Guzik: among other sins, the leaders killed faithful prophets and believers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
  - Matthew Henry: Nothing ripens a people more for ruin… than the sins of their priests and prophets. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_004.cfm
  - Guzik quotes Ellison that "bloodshed" covered more than murder. It included anything that robbed people of land and livelihood, and priests were guilty both by approving such things and by failing to condemn them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
- *Clarke (Methodist)* compares these leaders to the persecuting priests under Queen Mary in England. (Guzik URL)
- *Coffman* reads "even her prophets and priests": the whole nation was corrupt, and the leaders were the last ones left who might have been righteous. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/lamentations-4.html
- *Expositor's Bible:* the victims may have been men of the Jeremiah party. It compares the scene to fifteenth-century Rome, when popes and cardinals were the worst criminals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/lamentations/4.htm

**v. 14 — readings differ**
- Guzik: the people wander blind and defile themselves by stepping on dead bodies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
- Constable: some of the spiritually blind leaders may actually have lost their sight. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html
- Coffman: the priests were constantly made unclean by touching corpses, leaving the people without religious comfort. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/lamentations-4.html
- Clarke: better read "they ran frantic through the streets." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-4.html
- Expositor's suggests it may be a poetic picture of "moral lepers" rather than history. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/lamentations/4.htm

**v. 15**
- Constable: like lepers, they warn people away (Leviticus 13:45–46), and even pagan nations won't have them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html
- JFB: what a humiliation for Jews that Gentiles now shrank from touching them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/lamentations-4.html
- Calvin: they were sent away because their sins had made the holy city foul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/lamentations-4.html

**v. 16**
- Guzik: the sins of the priests and prophets (v. 13) brought on this loss of respect. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
- Constable: God scattered the leaders, and they had failed to honour the priests and elders. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html
- Coffman: the whole nation shared the guilt, not just the leaders. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/lamentations-4.html

**v. 17**
- Guzik: false prophets and politicians trusted Egypt to rescue them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
- Calvin: looking to false hopes instead of God was a sacrilege not to be endured. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/lamentations-4.html
- JFB: the wording shows they clung to hopes of Egypt even later, when Johanan led the remnant there. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/lamentations-4.html

**v. 18**
- *The usual reading:* Clarke and Wright (quoted by Guzik) say missiles from siege mounds and towers made the streets dangerous. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
- *Disagreement:* Keil and Delitzsch reject the siege-tower idea. The verb means to hunt down, so the picture comes from hunting. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/4-20.htm

**v. 19**
- Guzik: the Babylonians chased down anyone who fled, including King Zedekiah (Jeremiah 52:5–11). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/
- Keil: "in the wilderness" points to Zedekiah's capture (Jeremiah 39:5). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/4-20.htm

**v. 20 — the main point of disagreement**
- *Who is the king?*
  - Most say Zedekiah: Guzik, Matthew Henry and Constable. Constable notes that Zedekiah ended up blind and in prison. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-4/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html
  - Poole argues it can't be Josiah, who was killed in battle by the Egyptians, not captured. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/4-20.htm
  - The Geneva notes take it as Josiah, called anointed because he was a figure of Christ. (same URL)
  - JFB says it first referred to Josiah but is applied here to Zedekiah. (same URL)
  - Keil says it means the king's office as bearer of God's promise in 2 Samuel 7, not Zedekiah personally. (same URL)
- *Calvin (Reformed):* the people without their king were like a maimed body. The reality is found only in Christ, and the Church separated from Him is like a dead body. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/4-20.html
- *Gill (Baptist):* the words may be applied to Christ. He compares the disciples' lost hope when Jesus was crucified (Luke 24:21). He also notes that many early Christian writers applied the verse to Christ, and that Theodoret took it as a direct prophecy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/4-20.htm
- *Catholic translation:* the Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, reads The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord, is taken in our sins. https://biblehub.com/lamentations/4-20.htm
- *Lesson against trusting people:* Matthew Henry says that when we make any creature "the breath of our nostrils," God may justly take that breath away. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/4-20.html

**v. 21**
- Clarke: A strong irony. Edom joined the Babylonians, so it would share in the ruin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-4.html
- Constable quotes Harrison that Nebuchadnezzar gave rural Judah to Edom as a reward for its help. He says Uz was part of, near, or another name for Edom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html
- Calvin: the verse was meant to ease the grief of the godly and to call for patient endurance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/lamentations-4.html
- Expositor's: mentioning Uz shows how unusually prosperous Edom was. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/lamentations/4.htm

**v. 22 — traditions differ**
- *The usual reading:*
  - Constable: the punishment has reached its end, and the exile won't last forever. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-4.html
  - Matthew Henry: this is not the full punishment Zion deserved, but the full amount God had decided to give. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/4-22.html
  - Several note that "uncovering" sins means punishing them, as "covering" sins means forgiving them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/4-22.htm
- *Spurgeon (Baptist)* applies the verse to the cross: Christ hath for his people borne all the punishment which they deserved… God is satisfied, and asks no more. He also links Zion's pardon to sovereign grace and Edom's sentence to justice. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/a-message-from-god-for-thee
- *Clarke (Methodist)* reads it historically: Jerusalem's captivity would soon end. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/4-22.html
- *Did the promise hold, given the later Roman exile?*
  - Gill: it was fulfilled only partly, and finally refers to the Jews' future restoration. (same URL)
  - JFB: the Romans later took them away, so the full fulfilment points to their final restoration. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/lamentations-4.html
  - Ellicott: the promise had unstated conditions and was forfeited when the Jews rejected Christ. https://biblehub.com/lamentations/4-22.htm
  - Barnes: it doesn't promise Judah freedom from exile forever, only that this guilt is paid. https://www.studylight.org/bible/heb/hmd/lamentations/4-22.html
- *Jewish and scholarly readings:*
  - Keil says this passage is rightly called a "Messianic hope." The ancient Aramaic paraphrase (Targum) speaks of deliverance by the hands of the Messiah, and of Elias the high priest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/4-22.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/4-22.html
  - The NET Bible notes a wordplay: the same Hebrew word means Zion's "punishment," which is ending, and Edom's "sin," whose punishment is beginning. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=lam&chapter=4&verse=22

---

**What I couldn't find**
- No pages from the Catholic or Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org).
- Nothing from bibleodyssey.org.
- No distinct Lutheran or Pentecostal teaching on this chapter.
- No prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace material.

Those gaps may just mean I didn't search for them, not that nothing exists. The Catholic material above comes only from the Douay-Rheims wording, and the early-Church view of v. 20 only from Gill's report. Preceptaustin and Gill's full chapter are also worth checking before publishing.
